description: OkCupid's OkTrends data put average reply rates for male senders at Hispanic/Latino 25.2 against White 31.1, with Asian 25.3 and Black 22.6. Latino men sat near the middle-to-low end of the male sender hierarchy.
notes: 2009-2014 data, one platform. Recorded with that caveat.

aspect: EXAMPLE - and it held across five years
description: Christian Rudder examined interactions between 2009 and 2014 involving more than 25 million people using QuickMatch ratings; the biases stayed fairly consistent across the period.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the asymmetry with Latina women
description: The same data put Hispanic/Latina women as senders at 46.8, close to White women at 47.4 and above Black women at 36.3; Rudder found Latina women among those rated best. The nationality is read very differently depending on the sex of the person carrying it.
energy_note: The same origin helps her and costs him.

aspect: EXAMPLE - preemptive discrimination is the mechanism
description: Kevin Lewis, analysing over 126,000 OkCupid users, found people were more willing to reply across race lines than to initiate across them, and proposed that segregation occurs at the initiation stage because people anticipate rejection. The man does not message, because he expects not to hear back.
energy_note: He stops sending before anyone refuses him.

aspect: EXAMPLE - and it is habit, not fixed preference
description: Lewis found that receiving a cross-racial message made people significantly more likely to cross racial boundaries themselves afterwards - an effect lasting about a week. Stated preferences are also comparatively open: only about 15% of Latino men and 16% of Latina women stated a same-race preference.
energy_note: It moves, and it moves back within a week.

aspect: The caveats matter and are recorded
description: The OkTrends figures are 2009-2014, single-platform, and predate swipe interfaces. Pew (July 2022) found 30% of US adults had used a dating site with no statistically significant differences by race/ethnicity, so outcome gaps are not explained by who joins. An Oxford study across 24 countries found in-group preference ranging from under 20% in Chile to over 80% in Slovakia, pointing to culture rather than biology.
energy_note: Old data, one platform, and culturally contingent.
